title: CUET Mass Media Test 4
subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Mass Media - 318.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Mass Media papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: CBSE Mass Media Studies, Classes XI-XII (curriculum mirrored by the NTA syllabus)
Constitution of India, Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Acts and Supreme Court judgments as cited
Official histories of All India Radio, Doordarshan and Indian cinema
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a case; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The BBC begins a regular television service
(B) Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web
(C) Gutenberg's printing press
(D) Marconi's wireless experiments
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: Gutenberg's press dates from about 1450. Marconi's wireless experiments came in the 1890s. The BBC began regular TV in 1936, and the Web was proposed in 1989.
Why not the others: (A) puts TV before wireless. (B) puts Marconi before Gutenberg. (C) puts the Web before BBC TV.
Key point: Each new medium built on the technology before it.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question: The government institute in Pune that trains film-makers, actors and technicians is the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) FTII
Why: The Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), set up in 1960, trains people in film and TV.
Why not the others: (A) funds films. (B) certifies films. (C) is the National Film Archive, which preserves films.
Key point: Many parallel cinema directors and actors trained at FTII.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about television in India:
(A) Cable and satellite TV spread rapidly after the Gulf War coverage of 1991.
(B) Zee TV, launched in 1992, was started by Doordarshan.
(C) Prasar Bharati came into existence in 1997.
(D) DD News began as a 24-hour news channel in 2003.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Live satellite coverage of the 1991 Gulf War drove the cable boom, Prasar Bharati was formed in 1997, and DD News started in 2003.
Why not the others: (B) is false. Zee TV was a private channel, the first Hindi satellite channel run privately. Options (C) and (D) include (B), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: The 1990s ended Doordarshan's monopoly.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Translated text at the bottom of the screen
questions.question: A Malayalam film is shown in Delhi with the dialogue translated into English text at the bottom of the screen. This text is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Subtitles
Why: Subtitles give a written translation of the dialogue.
Why not the others: (B) list the people who made the film. (C) also describe sounds for viewers who cannot hear, not just translate. (D) replaces the spoken dialogue with another language.
Key point: Subtitles help films travel across languages.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Advertising that hides the product at first
questions.question: A campaign that shows posters saying only "Something new is coming on 1 May", without naming the product, is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Teaser campaign
Why: A teaser campaign holds back the product's name to build curiosity before the launch.
Why not the others: (A) corrects a false impression. (B) reminds buyers of a known product. (C) promotes a social cause.
Key point: Teasers make people wait for the reveal.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Sharing the cost of an advertisement
questions.question: A phone maker and a local shop share the cost of a newspaper advertisement that shows the phone and the shop's address. This is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cooperative advertising
Why: In cooperative advertising two parties, often a maker and a seller, share the cost.
Why not the others: (A) promotes a company's image. (C) compares brands. (D) promotes a banned product through another item.
Key point: Cooperative advertising helps both the brand and the shop.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Lobbying
(B) Spin
(C) Media relations
(D) Community relations

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Building good contacts with journalists
(II) Keeping good ties with the people who live around a factory or office
(III) Presenting facts in a slanted way to favour a client
(IV) Trying to influence lawmakers and officials
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Lobbying tries to influence lawmakers (IV). Spin slants facts (III). Media relations means dealing with journalists (I), and community relations means good ties with neighbours (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps lobbying and spin. (B) swaps spin and media relations. (C) swaps media and community relations.
Key point: PR deals with many publics: government, media and community.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: Journalism that uses shocking headlines, scandal and exaggeration to sell copies, with little regard for facts, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Yellow journalism
Why: Yellow journalism relies on sensation and scandal rather than careful reporting.
Why not the others: (A) covers development issues. (B) digs out hidden wrongdoing with research. (C) openly argues for a cause.
Key point: The name comes from a cartoon, "The Yellow Kid", in rival American papers of the 1890s.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Influencer
(B) Meme
(C) Livestream
(D) Story

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A post that disappears after 24 hours
(II) Video broadcast as it happens
(III) A person with a large following who shapes opinions
(IV) A funny image or idea that spreads widely
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: An influencer has a large following (III). A meme is a humorous idea that spreads (IV). A livestream is real-time video (II), and a story disappears after 24 hours (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps influencer and meme. (B) swaps meme and livestream. (D) swaps livestream and story.
Key point: Social media has its own formats and vocabulary.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Facial expressions, gestures and posture are forms of ____ communication.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) non-verbal
Why: Non-verbal communication sends messages without words, through the face, the body and movement.
Why not the others: (B) uses words. (A) and (D) are levels of communication, not kinds of signal.
Key point: Non-verbal signals often say more than words.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question: In an advertisement, the written words, such as the headline and the text, are called the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) copy
Why: Copy is the text of an advertisement, written by a copywriter.
Why not the others: (B) is the arrangement of elements. (C) is the picture. (D) is the brand's symbol.
Key point: Copy and visual work together in an advertisement.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: When a listener interprets the words and signs a speaker has used and works out their meaning, the process is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Decoding
Why: Decoding is the receiver's work of turning the code back into meaning.
Why not the others: (A) is the sender putting an idea into a code. (B) is sending the message through a channel. (C) is the receiver's response.
Key point: Encoding and decoding must use a shared code.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.sub_topic: What mass communication does not do
questions.question: The mass media serve several purposes in society. Which one of these is NOT among them?
options: A) Informing people about events at home and abroad
C) Making everyone hold the same opinion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Making everyone hold the same opinion
Why: The mass media inform, educate, entertain and help people discuss issues. Forcing everyone to agree is not a function and would harm democracy.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are standard functions of mass communication.
Key point: Inform, educate and entertain are the three classic functions.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: How a film reaches its audience
questions.question:
Arrange the following in the order in which a finished film reaches the public:
(A) The exhibitor screens it in a cinema hall
(B) The producer completes the film
(C) The audience buys tickets and watches it
(D) The distributor acquires the rights and supplies prints
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: The producer completes the film. A distributor buys the rights and supplies it to cinemas. The exhibitor screens it, and the audience watches.
Why not the others: (A) screens before distribution. (C) distributes before the film is made. (D) has the audience watch before it is screened.
Key point: Producer, distributor and exhibitor are the three links of the film trade.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: What Article 19(2) does not allow as a limit
questions.question: Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions on free speech. Which of the following is NOT a ground for such a restriction?
options: A) Friendly relations with foreign States
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Criticism of the government
Why: Criticising the government is protected speech. It is not a ground for restriction under Article 19(2).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are among the grounds listed in Article 19(2).
Key point: Freedom of the press includes the freedom to criticise those in power.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: An agency that supplies news to many papers
questions.question: The Press Trust of India, which supplies news to many newspapers and channels, is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) News agency
Why: A news agency gathers news and sells it to many media outlets. PTI is India's largest.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) publish or broadcast to the public. (C) regulates the press.
Key point: Agencies let small papers carry news from far away.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Deepfake
(B) Algorithm
(C) Paywall
(D) Podcast

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A realistic fake video made with artificial intelligence
(II) An audio programme that can be played on demand
(III) A barrier that asks readers to pay to see content
(IV) A set of rules that decides what a user sees
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: A deepfake is an AI-made fake video (I). An algorithm decides what a user sees (IV). A paywall asks for payment (III), and a podcast is on-demand audio (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps deepfake and algorithm. (B) swaps algorithm and paywall. (C) swaps paywall and podcast.
Key point: New media brings new tools and new risks.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Rule of thirds
(B) Candid photograph
(C) Photo essay
(D) Cropping

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A picture taken without the subject posing
(II) Cutting away unwanted parts of a picture
(III) Placing the subject along lines that divide the frame into nine parts
(IV) A series of pictures that tells a story
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: The rule of thirds places the subject along grid lines (III). A candid photo is unposed (I). A photo essay tells a story in a series (IV), and cropping trims a picture (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the rule of thirds and candid photo. (B) swaps candid photo and photo essay. (D) swaps photo essay and cropping.
Key point: Photojournalists tell stories through composition and selection.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: How a TV news story reaches the screen
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in the making of a TV news report in the correct order:
(A) The edited report is played out during the bulletin
(B) The reporter and camera person shoot at the spot
(C) The assignment desk sends a reporter to the event
(D) The footage is edited and a voice-over is added
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: The assignment desk sends a crew, the crew shoots at the spot, the footage is edited with a voice-over, and the report goes on air.
Why not the others: (A) shoots before anyone is assigned. (B) edits before shooting. (D) airs the report before it is edited.
Key point: News production runs from assignment to playout.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about social media:
(A) It helps people with shared interests form communities across distances.
(B) It gives marginalised groups a way to raise their concerns.
(C) Its algorithms show every user exactly the same feed.
(D) Political parties use it to reach voters directly.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. Algorithms personalise each feed, choosing posts based on a user's past activity.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Personalised feeds can create echo chambers.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Advertising Standards Council of India was set up in 1985.
(B) ASCI is a government ministry that can send advertisers to jail.
(C) Advertising revenue pays for much of the cost of newspapers and TV.
(D) Advertising tells consumers about new products.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false. ASCI is a voluntary, self-regulatory body set up by the advertising industry; it cannot jail anyone.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: ASCI regulates advertising from within the industry.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.question: YouTube is best described as a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Video-sharing platform
Why: YouTube lets users upload, watch and share videos.
Why not the others: (A) carries short text posts. (C) is for careers. (D) is for private chats.
Key point: Video sharing is one of the main types of social media.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: A second check when logging in
questions.question: A user enters her password and then a one-time code sent to her phone before she can log in. This safety measure is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Two-factor authentication
Why: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof of identity besides the password, which protects against hacking.
Why not the others: (A) scrambles data so that others cannot read it. (B) blocks unwanted network traffic. (D) are small files websites store on a device.
Key point: A stolen password alone cannot open an account protected this way.

questions.topic: Social Media
questions.sub_topic: A misleading headline that lures clicks
questions.question: A headline such as "You won't believe what this actor did next!", written mainly to make people click, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Clickbait
Why: Clickbait uses teasing or misleading headlines to attract clicks, often with little real content.
Why not the others: (B) groups posts by topic. (C) is a humorous image that spreads. (D) is good behaviour online.
Key point: Clickbait trades accuracy for traffic.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: A story that is not hard news
questions.question: A long article about the life of a village potter, written to interest and move readers rather than to report a breaking event, is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Feature
Why: A feature is a soft, human-interest story with more depth and colour than a news report.
Why not the others: (A) is a short news item. (C) gives the paper's opinion. (D) is material sent by an organisation.
Key point: Features need not be tied to a breaking event.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: A job that is not the PRO's
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually a job of an organisation's public relations officer (PRO)?
options: B) Editing a newspaper's front page
D) Handling the media in a crisis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Editing a newspaper's front page
Why: Editing a newspaper is the work of journalists, not of the organisation's PRO.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are all duties of a PRO.
Key point: The PRO speaks for the organisation to the media and public.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: Aristotle's model of communication is mainly concerned with:
options: A) Noise in a technical channel
B) A speaker persuading an audience
C) Feedback in a circular exchange
D) The role of the gatekeeper
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A speaker persuading an audience
Why: Aristotle's model centres on the speaker, the speech and the audience, and on how a speaker persuades through character, emotion and reason.
Why not the others: (A) is Shannon and Weaver's idea. (C) belongs to circular models. (D) belongs to Westley and MacLean.
Key point: Aristotle's is the oldest model and is speaker-centred.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question: A small space on the front page kept for news that arrives after the rest of the page is ready is called the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) stop press
Why: The stop press carries late news inserted just before printing.
Why not the others: (A) is the paper's name at the top. (B) is a small box beside the masthead. (D) gives the place and date of a story.
Key point: The stop press is the last thing added to a page.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Newspaper)
(A) Mirat-ul-Akhbar
(B) Bombay Samachar
(C) The Hindu
(D) Al-Hilal

List-II (Founder)
(I) G. Subramania Iyer and associates
(II) Raja Ram Mohan Roy
(III) Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
(IV) Fardunji Marzban
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Ram Mohan Roy started the Persian paper Mirat-ul-Akhbar in 1822 (II). Fardunji Marzban began Bombay Samachar the same year (IV). The Hindu was founded in 1878 by G. Subramania Iyer and his associates (I), and Azad started Al-Hilal in 1912 (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two. (C) swaps Bombay Samachar and The Hindu. (D) swaps The Hindu and Al-Hilal.
Key point: Reformers and nationalists used newspapers to reach the public.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: The study of body movements, gestures and facial expressions as communication is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Kinesics
Why: Kinesics is the study of body language.
Why not the others: (B) studies the use of space and distance. (C) studies the use of time. (D) studies the meaning of words.
Key point: Kinesics is one branch of non-verbal communication.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: A folder of material for journalists
questions.question: A folder handed to journalists at a launch, containing a press release, photos, fact sheets and contact details, is called a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Press kit
Why: A press kit (media kit) gives journalists everything they need to write the story.
Why not the others: (A) is a magazine for employees. (B) is the agency's plan for placing advertisements. (D) is a booklet for customers.
Key point: The press kit is a standard PR tool.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Where sets are built and lit
questions.question: A large building in which sets are built and scenes are shot under controlled lighting is called a film:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Studio
Why: A film studio provides space, sets and lighting for shooting.
Why not the others: (A) preserves films. (B) is a club that screens films. (D) is an event that shows films.
Key point: Shooting is done in a studio or on location.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.sub_topic: Terms used on a film set
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Clapperboard
(B) Rushes
(C) Final cut
(D) Location

List-II (Meaning)
(I) The footage shot on a single day, viewed soon after
(II) A board snapped shut to match sound with picture
(III) A real place outside the studio where scenes are shot
(IV) The finished edited version of the film
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: The clapperboard helps match sound and picture (II). Rushes are each day's footage (I). The final cut is the finished film (IV), and a location is a real place used for shooting (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps clapperboard and rushes. (C) swaps rushes and final cut. (D) swaps final cut and location.
Key point: Each term belongs to a stage of the production process.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question: A newspaper that puts its stories on its website and app as soon as they are ready, and prints them the next morning, follows a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Digital-first policy
Why: Digital-first means publishing online first and treating print as a later edition.
Why not the others: (A) ignores online publication. (C) is about charging readers. (D) concerns TV and radio.
Key point: Convergence has pushed news organisations to go digital-first.

questions.topic: Communication: levels, models, culture, social change and the evolution of media
questions.question: The Kheda Communication Project (1975), in which local TV programmes were made with and for villagers in Gujarat, is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Development communication
Why: The Kheda project, run by ISRO, used television to help villagers with farming, health and social issues. This is development communication.
Why not the others: (A) aims at profit. (C) promotes a party or government line. (D) builds a company's image.
Key point: Kheda involved villagers in making the programmes they watched.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question: Narration heard over the pictures by a speaker who is not seen on screen is called a ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) voice-over
Why: A voice-over is spoken over the visuals by an unseen narrator.
Why not the others: (A) is the reporter speaking on camera. (C) is a short clip of someone speaking. (D) is a report given over the phone.
Key point: The voice-over is recorded and added during editing.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Deciding guilt before the court does
questions.question: When news coverage treats an accused person as guilty before the court has given its verdict, it is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Trial by media
Why: Trial by media is coverage that prejudges guilt and may harm a fair trial.
Why not the others: (B) concerns disrespect to Parliament. (C) is selecting which news to publish. (D) is the media deciding which issues people think about.
Key point: An accused person is innocent until proven guilty.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Press Council of India:
(A) It is a statutory, quasi-judicial body working under the Press Council Act, 1978.
(B) By convention, its chairperson is a retired judge of the Supreme Court.
(C) It regulates television news channels as well as newspapers.
(D) It hears complaints against the press and complaints by the press.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. The Council works under the 1978 Act, is headed by a retired Supreme Court judge, and hears complaints both against newspapers and from journalists whose freedom is threatened.
Why not the others: (C) is false. The Council covers the print media only, not television. Options (B) and (C) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: The Press Council guards both press freedom and press standards.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The hours with the biggest audience
questions.question: The evening hours when the largest number of people watch TV, and advertising costs the most, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Prime time
Why: Prime time is the peak viewing period, usually in the evening.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) draw smaller audiences.
Key point: Channels place their strongest programmes in prime time.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Transition)
(A) Cut
(B) Dissolve
(C) Fade
(D) Wipe

List-II (Effect)
(I) An instant change from one shot to the next
(II) The picture slowly goes to or comes from black
(III) One shot gradually blends into the next
(IV) A new shot pushes the old one off the screen along a line
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: A cut is instant (I). A dissolve blends one shot into the next (III). A fade goes to or from black (II), and a wipe pushes across the screen (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps cut and dissolve. (C) swaps dissolve and fade. (D) swaps fade and wipe.
Key point: Transitions are added at the editing stage.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question: The internet is often described as a network of ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) networks
Why: The internet links millions of smaller computer networks around the world.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) may use the internet but are not what it is made of.
Key point: The internet is where all media now meet.

questions.topic: TV Production Process and Programmes
questions.sub_topic: The presenter of a news bulletin
questions.question: The person who presents a news bulletin on TV and links its stories together is called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Anchor
Why: The anchor presents the bulletin, reads the links and talks to reporters and guests.
Why not the others: (A) plans and runs the programme. (B) operates the camera. (C) passes on the director's instructions.
Key point: The anchor is the face of a news programme.

questions.topic: Cinema: history, production process, genres and cinema for social change
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about documentary films:
(A) Films Division was set up in 1978 to fund commercial feature films.
(B) A documentary may use narration, interviews and archive footage.
(C) An observational documentary avoids narration and lets events unfold.
(D) A documentary may re-create past events when no footage of them exists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) are correct. Documentaries draw on many kinds of material, observational films simply watch, and reconstructions are used when no footage exists.
Why not the others: (A) is false. Films Division was set up in 1948 to make documentaries and newsreels for the government. Options (A) and (B) include (A), and (C) leaves out (C).
Key point: Documentaries have many styles, but all deal with reality.

questions.topic: New Media
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about new media:
(A) Leaders can speak directly to citizens through social media.
(B) Online campaigns have no effect on decisions taken offline.
(C) Fact-checking websites have grown to counter fake news.
(D) Readers can no longer comment on news.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A) and (C) only
Why: (A) and (C) are correct. Social media lets leaders bypass the press, and fact-checkers have grown in response to fake news.
Why not the others: (B) is false, since online campaigns often push authorities to act. (D) is false, since new media lets readers comment and share. Options (A), (B) and (D) include a false statement.
Key point: New media has changed how citizens, leaders and journalists interact.

questions.topic: Journalism: news, the journalist, reporting and editing, photojournalism, media laws and ethics
questions.sub_topic: Ranks in a newspaper's editorial team
questions.question:
Arrange the following posts in a newspaper's editorial department from the highest to the lowest:
(A) Sub-editor
(B) News editor
(C) Editor
(D) Chief sub-editor
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: The editor heads the paper. The news editor runs the news desk, the chief sub-editor leads a shift of sub-editors, and sub-editors edit the copy.
Why not the others: (B) puts the news editor above the editor. (C) puts the chief sub-editor above the news editor. (D) puts the sub-editor above the chief sub-editor.
Key point: Copy passes up this chain before it is printed.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi produces a weekly farm programme at an All India Radio station. An agricultural scientist sends him a script on fertiliser use for paddy. It begins: "The application of nitrogenous fertiliser in split doses at 21 and 45 days after transplanting is recommended for optimal yield, subject to soil-test values."

Ravi rewrites it. In his version, a young farmer, Basappa, chats with an expert, "Doctor-avaru". Basappa asks the questions listeners might ask: "How much should I put? When?" The expert answers in short, everyday sentences. The programme opens with the sound of bullock bells and birds in a field. At the end, the expert sums up the main advice once more.

In the studio, the two speakers sit facing each other across a small table, with a single microphone placed between them that picks up sound from the front and the back but not from the sides.

Question: The scientist's opening sentence is poor radio writing mainly because a radio script should be:
options: A) Formal, like a research paper
C) Conversational, like talking to a friend
D) Written in long and detailed sentences
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Conversational, like talking to a friend
Why: Radio is heard, not read, and listeners feel spoken to one at a time. A good radio script sounds like natural talk.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) describe the scientist's script, which is written for the eye.
Key point: Write for radio the way you would speak to a friend.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Why the advice is summed up again
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi produces a weekly farm programme at an All India Radio station. An agricultural scientist sends him a script on fertiliser use for paddy. It begins: "The application of nitrogenous fertiliser in split doses at 21 and 45 days after transplanting is recommended for optimal yield, subject to soil-test values."

Ravi rewrites it. In his version, a young farmer, Basappa, chats with an expert, "Doctor-avaru". Basappa asks the questions listeners might ask: "How much should I put? When?" The expert answers in short, everyday sentences. The programme opens with the sound of bullock bells and birds in a field. At the end, the expert sums up the main advice once more.

In the studio, the two speakers sit facing each other across a small table, with a single microphone placed between them that picks up sound from the front and the back but not from the sides.

Question: Why does the expert repeat the main advice at the end of the programme?
options: A) Listeners cannot go back, and some tune in late
B) Radio rules require every point to be said twice
C) It fills time when the script runs short
D) Repetition is needed for the recording to be edited
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Listeners cannot go back, and some tune in late
Why: A listener cannot re-read what was missed, and some join the programme midway. Repeating the key points helps them remember.
Why not the others: (B) is not a rule. (C) and (D) are not the reasons for a planned summary.
Key point: In radio, repetition is a strength, not a fault.

Ravi rewrites it. In his version, a young farmer, Basappa, chats with an expert, "Doctor-avaru". Basappa asks the questions listeners might ask: "How much should I put? When?" The expert answers in short, everyday sentences. The programme opens with the sound of bullock bells and birds in a field. At the end, the expert sums up the main advice once more.

In the studio, the two speakers sit facing each other across a small table, with a single microphone placed between them that picks up sound from the front and the back but not from the sides.

Question: The sound of bullock bells and birds at the start of the programme is used mainly to:
options: A) Cover up a fault in the recording
C) Fill the silence before the news
D) Set the scene in the listener's mind
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Set the scene in the listener's mind
Why: Sound effects create a picture of the setting, here a village field, so that the listener imagines where the talk is taking place.
Why not the others: (A) is not their purpose. (B) is the job of a jingle or station ident. (C) is not suggested in the case.
Key point: Sound effects help radio paint pictures.

questions.sub_topic: One microphone for two speakers facing each other
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi produces a weekly farm programme at an All India Radio station. An agricultural scientist sends him a script on fertiliser use for paddy. It begins: "The application of nitrogenous fertiliser in split doses at 21 and 45 days after transplanting is recommended for optimal yield, subject to soil-test values."

Ravi rewrites it. In his version, a young farmer, Basappa, chats with an expert, "Doctor-avaru". Basappa asks the questions listeners might ask: "How much should I put? When?" The expert answers in short, everyday sentences. The programme opens with the sound of bullock bells and birds in a field. At the end, the expert sums up the main advice once more.

In the studio, the two speakers sit facing each other across a small table, with a single microphone placed between them that picks up sound from the front and the back but not from the sides.

Question: The single microphone that picks up sound from the front and the back, but not from the sides, is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bidirectional microphone
Why: A bidirectional microphone has a figure-of-eight pattern. It picks up from front and back, so it suits two people sitting face to face.
Why not the others: (A) picks up mainly from the front. (C) picks up from all sides, including room noise. (D) picks up a narrow area in one direction.
Key point: The pick-up pattern should match where the speakers sit.

questions.topic: Radio: writing for radio and radio recording
questions.sub_topic: Why Ravi turned the talk into a chat
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Ravi produces a weekly farm programme at an All India Radio station. An agricultural scientist sends him a script on fertiliser use for paddy. It begins: "The application of nitrogenous fertiliser in split doses at 21 and 45 days after transplanting is recommended for optimal yield, subject to soil-test values."

Ravi rewrites it. In his version, a young farmer, Basappa, chats with an expert, "Doctor-avaru". Basappa asks the questions listeners might ask: "How much should I put? When?" The expert answers in short, everyday sentences. The programme opens with the sound of bullock bells and birds in a field. At the end, the expert sums up the main advice once more.

In the studio, the two speakers sit facing each other across a small table, with a single microphone placed between them that picks up sound from the front and the back but not from the sides.

Question: What is the main advantage of Ravi turning the scientist's talk into a chat between Basappa and the expert?
options: A) It removes the need for an expert on the programme
B) It allows the programme to run without a script
C) It makes the programme shorter than a talk
D) Listeners hear their own questions being asked
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Listeners hear their own questions being asked
Why: Basappa speaks for the listeners. When he asks "How much? When?", farmers hear their own doubts answered, which makes the advice easier to follow and trust.
Why not the others: (A) is wrong, as the expert still gives the advice. (B) is wrong, since Ravi wrote the chat. (C) is not stated and is not the point.
Key point: The dialogue format turns a lecture into a conversation listeners can relate to.
